questions.stem: A 50-year-old female is presenting to the gynecology OPD with abdominal distention and reduced appetite. Her physical examination revealed the presence of moderate ascites, and an ultrasound revealed the presence of an ovarian mass. The ascitic fluid was tapped, revealing elevated CA 125 and the presence of malignant cells. Genetic analysis of the cells showed increased activity of the telomerase enzyme. The enzyme promotes cell growth by which of the following actions?

options.label: D
options.text: Promotion of G1 to S progression

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Prevention of chromosome shortening

 

Telomerase is an enzyme that adds repetitive nucleotide sequences to the ends of chromosomes, known as telomeres. In normal cells, telomeres shorten with each cell division, eventually leading to cellular aging and death. Telomerase counteracts this process by preventing the shortening of telomeres, thereby allowing cells to continue dividing indefinitely.

 

In cancer cells, telomerase is often overactive, which allows the cells to bypass normal limits on cell division, contributing to the immortality of these malignant cells. This is a key feature in many cancers, including ovarian cancer, as seen in this patient. The patient's clinical presentation, coupled with the elevated CA 125 and the detection of malignant cells, supports a diagnosis of ovarian carcinoma, in which telomerase activity plays a significant role in promoting cancer cell proliferation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Enhancing tissue invasion and metastasis: This option describes mechanisms involved in cancer metastasis, such as the breakdown of extracellular matrix and invasion into surrounding tissues, but it is not the direct role of telomerase. Telomerase is primarily involved in preventing chromosome shortening, not tissue invasion.

 

Option C. Enhanced transcription factor expression: This option refers to the role of oncogenes, such as MYC, which drive cancer by promoting the expression of genes involved in cell growth. However, this is not the direct action of telomerase. Telomerase focuses on maintaining telomere length, not on enhancing transcription factor expression.

 

Option D. Promotion of G1 to S progression: The transition from G1 to S phase in the cell cycle is primarily regulated by cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), not by telomerase. Although G1 to S progression is critical for cell proliferation, it is not the specific mechanism by which telomerase promotes cell growth.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Telomerase prevents chromosome shortening, allowing cancer cells to divide indefinitely, which contributes to their immortality.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not properly matched?

options.label: A
options.text: Anaphylaxis on blood transfusion: IgA deficiency

options.label: B
options.text: Decreased B cells and T cells due to adenosine deaminase: SCID

options.label: C
options.text: Defective CD40L and CD40 interaction: class switching defect

options.label: D
options.text: Cardiac defects, absent thymic shadow X ray, hypercalcemia: DiGeorge syndrome

questions.answerText: Cardiac defects, absent thymic shadow X ray, hypercalcemia: DiGeorge syndrome
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Cardiac defects, absent thymic shadow on X-ray, hypercalcemia: DiGeorge syndrome

 

DiGeorge syndrome, a genetic disorder caused by a deletion on chromosome 22q11.2, is characterized by several classic features including congenital cardiac defects, absent or hypoplastic thymus (leading to an absent thymic shadow on X-ray), and hypocalcemia (due to parathyroid hypoplasia). The inclusion of hypercalcemia in the question is incorrect, as patients with DiGeorge syndrome typically experience hypocalcemia due to the underdevelopment of the parathyroid glands, not hypercalcemia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Anaphylaxis on blood transfusion: IgA deficiency: This is correctly matched. Individuals with IgA deficiency may develop anaphylactic reactions during blood transfusions because their immune system can produce anti-IgA antibodies, which react to the IgA in the transfused blood, causing anaphylaxis.

 

Option B. Decreased B cells and T cells due to adenosine deaminase: SCID: This is also correctly matched. Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) can result from a deficiency in the enzyme adenosine deaminase (ADA). This deficiency leads to a toxic buildup of metabolites that result in the decreased function or absence of both B and T cells.

 

Option C. Defective CD40L and CD40 interaction: class switching defect: This is correctly matched as well. A defect in the CD40L (ligand) and CD40 interaction leads to a class-switching defect, resulting in Hyper-IgM syndrome, where the patient is unable to switch from producing IgM to other immunoglobulin classes such as IgG, IgA, or IgE.

 

Educational Objective:

 

DiGeorge syndrome is associated with cardiac defects, absent thymic shadow, and hypocalcemia—not hypercalcemia.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presented in the OPD with abdominal discomfort and was found to have enlarged lymph nodes. Multiple investigations revealed the diagnosis of lymphoma. Combination chemotherapy was prescribed, and after 3 to 4 cycles, there was a significant reduction in the size of the affected nodes. The biopsy of the nodes revealed the presence of shrunken eosinophilic cells within the tumor. Which of the following substances released from the mitochondria has triggered the change observed in the biopsy?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Cytochrome c

 

The biopsy of the lymph nodes showing shrunken eosinophilic cells is indicative of apoptosis. Apoptosis, or programmed cell death, is a process by which cells are systematically dismantled and removed without causing an inflammatory response.

 

Chemotherapy often triggers apoptosis in cancer cells, leading to tumor reduction. In the intrinsic pathway of apoptosis, one of the key events is the release of cytochrome c from the mitochondria into the cytoplasm. Cytochrome c then binds to APAF-1 (apoptosis-activating factor 1), leading to the formation of the apoptosome, which in turn activates caspase 9, initiating a cascade of caspase activations that execute apoptosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. FAS: FAS is involved in the extrinsic pathway of apoptosis, not the intrinsic pathway seen here. FAS (CD95) binds to its ligand (FASL) on the cell surface, leading to the activation of caspases 8 and 10. However, this is not the pathway triggered by mitochondrial release of cytochrome c, which is characteristic of the intrinsic pathway.

 

Option C. Superoxide dismutase: Superoxide dismutase is an antioxidant enzyme that helps neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS) and protects cells from oxidative damage. While oxidative stress can play a role in apoptosis, superoxide dismutase itself is not involved in the direct triggering of apoptosis via mitochondrial release of cytochrome c.

 

Option D. Caspases: Caspases are indeed involved in apoptosis, but they are activated downstream in the process. Cytochrome c release from mitochondria is the initiating event that triggers caspase activation, starting with caspase 9 in the intrinsic pathway. Caspases alone do not initiate the process; they execute apoptosis once the pathway is triggered.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cytochrome c released from the mitochondria is a key trigger in the intrinsic pathway of apoptosis, leading to the activation of caspases and programmed cell death.

questions.stem: Enamel-like superstructure is seen in which of the following CNS lesions?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Craniopharyngioma

 

Craniopharyngioma is a benign tumor that arises from remnants of Rathke's pouch, an embryonic structure that contributes to the development of the pituitary gland. This tumor is often found in the suprasellar region and is more commonly seen in children and young adults.

 

A hallmark of craniopharyngioma is the presence of both solid and cystic components. Additionally, these tumors often contain calcifications, which can be described as tooth-like or enamel-like structures. This characteristic calcification is a key feature that distinguishes craniopharyngioma from other CNS lesions.

 

Another clue to the diagnosis of craniopharyngioma is the presence of a dark brown, oily fluid within the cystic component, sometimes referred to as having a machine oil-like appearance.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Pituitary tumor: Pituitary tumors generally arise from the glandular tissue of the pituitary and do not exhibit the characteristic enamel-like or tooth-like calcifications seen in craniopharyngiomas. They are more commonly associated with hormonal disturbances and mass effects on nearby structures, such as the optic chiasm.

 

Option C. Astrocytoma: Astrocytomas are glial cell tumors that can occur throughout the CNS. They do not typically have the enamel-like calcifications that are a feature of craniopharyngiomas. Instead, astrocytomas tend to be infiltrative and cause neurological symptoms based on their location.

 

Option D. Glioma: Gliomas are a broad category of tumors that arise from glial cells and include astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, and others. Like astrocytomas, they do not have enamel-like calcifications and are more known for their invasive growth patterns rather than distinctive calcific structures.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following conditions has the graph depicted by the red line? Sickle cell anemiaAutoimmune hemolytic anemiaHereditary spherocytosisThalassemia
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 2 and 3

 

The red line in the graph represents an increase in osmotic fragility. This means that the red blood cells (RBCs) in this condition are more prone to lysis when exposed to decreasing concentrations of NaCl (hypotonic solutions).

 

In conditions where the RBCs have altered shapes, such as being more spherical or more fragile, the osmotic fragility increases, causing them to burst at higher concentrations of NaCl compared to normal cells.

 

2. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) can also lead to increased osmotic fragility as the immune-mediated destruction of RBC membranes makes them more fragile.

 

3. Hereditary spherocytosis is characterized by the presence of spherical RBCs due to a defect in the cytoskeletal proteins. These spherical cells are less deformable and more fragile, leading to increased osmotic fragility, which is what the red line represents.

 

Other Options:

 

1. Sickle cell anemia: Sickle cell anemia primarily involves RBCs that become sickle-shaped under low oxygen conditions. However, sickle cells tend to have decreased, not increased, osmotic fragility. Therefore, it does not match the condition represented by the red line.

 

4. Thalassemia: In thalassemia, there is defective hemoglobin production, but the cells do not necessarily show increased osmotic fragility as seen in hereditary spherocytosis or AIHA. Thalassemia is more associated with ineffective erythropoiesis and hemolysis rather than increased osmotic fragility.

 

Educational Objective:

questions.stem: The phlebotomist needs to collect samples from a patient for various tests. Among the options provided, which sequence of blood collection for testing ensures that the sample remains uncontaminated, considering the additives present in the collection tubes?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Light blue → Red → Lavender → Grey

 

In blood sample collection, it is essential to follow a specific order of draw to prevent cross-contamination between the additives present in different collection tubes. If not followed, the results of the tests could be compromised. The correct order of draw minimizes the risk of additive carryover and ensures sample integrity.

 

The correct sequence based on the additives is as follows:

 

  1. Light blue (Citrate tube): This tube is used for coagulation studies and must be drawn first to avoid contamination by other additives, especially clot activators or EDTA, which could interfere with clotting times.
  2. Red (Serum tube): These tubes are either plain or have clot activators but contain no anticoagulants. Drawing the serum tube after the light blue tube ensures that coagulation tests are unaffected.
  3. Lavender (EDTA tube): EDTA is a potent anticoagulant used for hematology tests (e.g., complete blood count). If drawn earlier, EDTA could interfere with coagulation or serum tests.
  4. Grey (Fluoride/Oxalate tube): This tube contains sodium fluoride, which inhibits glycolysis, and is typically used for glucose testing. It must be drawn last to prevent contamination with anticoagulants that could affect other tests.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Light blue → Lavender → Red → Grey: This sequence is incorrect because the lavender (EDTA) tube is drawn before the red (serum) tube. EDTA could contaminate the serum sample, potentially affecting the test results.

 

Option C. Grey → Red → Light blue → Lavender: This sequence is incorrect because the grey tube should always be drawn last to prevent contamination of other samples. Additionally, the light blue tube should be drawn before the red or lavender tubes.

 

Option D. Red → Lavender → Grey → Light blue: This sequence is incorrect because the light blue (citrate) tube for coagulation studies should always be drawn first. Additionally, the grey tube should be drawn last.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The correct sequence of blood sample collection is Light blue → Red → Lavender → Grey, ensuring proper sample integrity and avoiding contamination by additives from different tubes.
  • Standard Order of Draw (by CLSI guidelines):
    • Blood culture bottles (if ordered)
    • Light blue – Sodium citrate (coagulation studies like PT, aPTT)
    • Red or gold – No additive or clot activator (serum tests)
    • Green – Heparin (chemistry tests)
    • Lavender or pink – EDTA (CBC, blood bank)
    • Grey – Fluoride oxalate (glucose, lactate)

questions.stem: Which of the statements below accurately pertain to amyloidosis? It is an extracellular protein.Apple green birefringence is seen with Congo red under polarized microscopy.Beta-pleated sheets are seen on X-ray crystallography.AL is a secondary type of amyloidosis.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 1, 2, 3

 

Amyloidosis is a group of diseases characterized by the deposition of abnormal protein aggregates, known as amyloid, in various tissues and organs. The characteristics of amyloidosis are as follows:

 

1. It is an extracellular protein: Amyloid is deposited in the extracellular space of tissues, where it disrupts normal organ function. This is a fundamental feature of amyloidosis.

 

2. Apple green birefringence is seen with Congo red under polarized microscopy: Amyloid deposits show a characteristic apple-green birefringence when stained with Congo red and viewed under polarized light. This is a diagnostic hallmark of amyloidosis.

 

3. Beta-pleated sheets are seen on X-ray crystallography: The abnormal amyloid fibrils adopt a beta-pleated sheet structure, which can be confirmed by X-ray crystallography. This structural arrangement contributes to the resistance of amyloid fibrils to proteolysis.

 

Other Option:

 

4. AL is a secondary type of amyloidosis: This statement is incorrect. AL amyloidosis, or amyloid light-chain amyloidosis, is a primary form of amyloidosis associated with plasma cell dyscrasias, such as multiple myeloma. Secondary amyloidosis (AA amyloidosis) is caused by chronic inflammatory conditions and involves the deposition of serum amyloid A (SAA) protein.

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 1-b, 2-d, 3-a, 4-c

 

Let’s break down the correct matching for each disorder with its associated genetic abnormality:

 

  1. Trinucleotide repeats → b. Fragile X syndrome: Fragile X syndrome is caused by a trinucleotide repeat expansion (CGG repeat) in the FMR1 gene, leading to intellectual disability, macroorchidism, and distinct facial features.
  2. Trisomy 18 → d. Edward syndrome: Trisomy 18 is associated with Edward syndrome, a condition that includes severe developmental delays, congenital heart defects, and distinct physical features.
  3. Trisomy 13 → a. Patau syndrome: Trisomy 13 is linked to Patau syndrome, which presents with severe congenital malformations, including cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, and central nervous system defects.
  4. Hb beta chain Glu → Val → c. Auto splenectomy: The substitution of glutamic acid to valine in the beta-globin chain is the hallmark of sickle cell anemia, where sickling of red blood cells can lead to complications like auto splenectomy (functional asplenia due to repeated infarctions of the spleen).

questions.stemHtml: Match the paraneoplastic syndromes with associated neoplasm:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 1-a, 2-d, 3-c, 4-b

 

  1. Cushing's syndrome → a. Small cell carcinoma of lung: Cushing's syndrome can occur as a paraneoplastic syndrome in patients with small cell carcinoma of the lung, which secretes ACTH or ACTH-like substances.
  2. Hypercalcemia → d. Squamous cell carcinoma of lung: Hypercalcemia can occur in patients with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung due to the production of parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP), leading to increased calcium levels.
  3. Polycythemia → c. Renal cell carcinoma: Renal cell carcinoma can produce erythropoietin, leading to increased red blood cell production and resulting in polycythemia.
  4. Acanthosis Nigricans → b. Gastric carcinoma: Acanthosis nigricans, a condition characterized by hyperpigmented, velvety skin lesions, is often associated with gastric carcinoma as a paraneoplastic syndrome.

questions.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman consults a doctor due to persistent malaise for five years and presents with high blood pressure. She passes away unexpectedly within a week. The autopsy reveals her kidneys' external and bisected appearance, as shown in the images. What is the most likely cause of her death?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Ruptured berry aneurysm

 

The images and the clinical history strongly suggest that the patient had autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). This condition is characterized by the presence of multiple cysts in both kidneys, which can lead to high blood pressure, kidney failure, and other complications. In ADPKD, one of the significant and potentially fatal complications is the development of berry aneurysms in the brain, which can rupture, leading to a subarachnoid hemorrhage or sudden death.

 

Key features supporting the diagnosis of ADPKD include:

 

  • The presence of multiple cysts on both kidneys (as seen in the image).
  • Hypertension, which is common in ADPKD due to kidney dysfunction.
  • The sudden death in the context of ADPKD is often due to complications such as the rupture of a berry aneurysm.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Metastatic Wilms tumor: Wilms tumor is primarily a pediatric malignancy, making this an unlikely cause of death in a 61-year-old woman. Moreover, the appearance of the kidneys with numerous cysts is not characteristic of Wilms tumor.

 

Option C. Acute tubular necrosis (ATN): While ATN is a common cause of acute kidney injury, it typically presents with signs of renal failure rather than sudden death. Additionally, the kidney appearance in ATN does not match the cystic changes seen in the provided images.

 

Option D. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC): DIC is a condition of abnormal clotting and bleeding, often secondary to other severe illnesses. It is not a typical complication of ADPKD and is unlikely to explain the findings in this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is associated with complications such as berry aneurysms, which can rupture and cause sudden death. This is a frequent cause of mortality in patients with ADPKD, making the rupture of a berry aneurysm the most likely cause of death in this patient.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old female presents to the emergency department with fever, hypotension, diffuse erythematous rash, and confusion. She reports recent use of tampons during menstruation. Laboratory studies reveal leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and elevated liver enzymes. Blood and urine cultures are obtained, and she is started on broad-spectrum antibiotics and intravenous fluids. Which of the following is true about the antigen involved here?

options.label: A
options.text: Binds to B7 and CD28 co-stimulatory molecules

options.label: B
options.text: Binds to the beta chain of TCR and MHC class II molecules of APC stimulating T cell activation

options.label: C
options.text: Binds to the CD4 + molecule causing T cell activation

options.label: D
options.text: Is presented by macrophages to a larger-than-normal number of T helper CD4 + lymphocytes

questions.answerText: Binds to the beta chain of TCR and MHC class II molecules of APC stimulating T cell activation
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Binds to the beta chain of TCR and MHC class II molecules of APC stimulating T cell activation

 

The patient's presentation is consistent with Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS), which is typically caused by Staphylococcus aureus (or less commonly, Streptococcus pyogenes) and is often associated with tampon use. The underlying cause of TSS is the production of a superantigen, which can lead to massive activation of T cells and a subsequent cytokine storm, resulting in symptoms such as fever, rash, hypotension, and multi-organ involvement.

 

A superantigen is unique in its mode of action, as it bypasses the usual antigen processing pathway. Instead of being processed and presented in the normal antigen-presenting cleft of the MHC class II molecule, the superantigen binds directly to the beta chain of the T-cell receptor (TCR) and the MHC class II molecule on antigen-presenting cells (APCs). This non-specific binding leads to the activation of a large number of T cells (up to 20% of all T cells), causing excessive cytokine release.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Binds to B7 and CD28 co-stimulatory molecules: This describes the normal co-stimulatory interaction between APCs and T cells, but it is not the mechanism by which superantigens operate.

 

Option C. Binds to the CD4+ molecule causing T cell activation: Superantigens do not bind directly to CD4 molecules. They interact with both the MHC class II molecule and TCR, leading to massive T cell activation.

 

Option D. Is presented by macrophages to a larger-than-normal number of T helper CD4+ lymphocytes: This statement partially describes the consequence of superantigen activity, but it does not explain the unique binding mechanism of superantigens to the TCR and MHC class II molecules, which is the key feature of their function.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Superantigens, such as those causing Toxic Shock Syndrome, bypass the normal antigen presentation process by binding directly to the beta chain of TCR and the MHC class II molecules, leading to excessive T cell activation and a cytokine storm.

questions.stem: In evaluating a patient with a suspected diagnosis of drug-induced lupus erythematosus (DILE), which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.label: B
options.text: Renal and CNS involvement is uncommon

options.label: C
options.text: Anti histone antibody levels are low

options.label: D
options.text: The disease remits after withdrawal of the offending drug

questions.answerText: Anti histone antibody levels are low
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Anti-histone antibody levels are low

 

Drug-induced lupus erythematosus (DILE) is a condition similar to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), but it is triggered by certain medications. It generally presents with mild systemic symptoms such as joint pain, fever, and fatigue, but it rarely involves severe organ systems like the kidneys or the central nervous system.

 

This statement is incorrect. In fact, the majority of patients with DILE have high levels of anti-histone antibodies, which are a hallmark of this condition. The presence of anti-histone antibodies is a distinguishing feature in drug-induced lupus.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Affects males and females equally: This is correct. Unlike SLE, which predominantly affects women, DILE affects men and women equally, as the gender bias seen in SLE is not as prominent in drug-induced forms of the disease.

 

Option B. Renal and CNS involvement is uncommon: This is correct. In DILE, renal and CNS involvement is rare, unlike in idiopathic SLE where these organ systems are often affected.

 

Option D. The disease remits after withdrawal of the offending drug: This is correct. DILE typically remits once the offending drug (commonly drugs like hydralazine, isoniazid, and procainamide) is stopped, and patients generally improve without further complications.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Anti-histone antibodies are typically high in drug-induced lupus erythematosus (DILE), and stopping the offending drug usually leads to remission of symptoms.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician with a 6-month history of fatigue, joint pain, and facial rash exacerbated by sun exposure. She also reports intermittent oral ulcers and hair loss. On physical examination, she has a malar rash over her cheeks and nasal bridge. Laboratory studies reveal anemia, leukopenia, lymphopenia, and elevated anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA). Which technique is most commonly used to identify autoantibodies?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Indirect immunofluorescence

 

The clinical presentation is consistent with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), an autoimmune disorder characterized by the presence of autoantibodies such as anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA). The indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) technique is the most commonly used method for detecting ANAs in SLE.

 

Indirect immunofluorescence involves adding patient serum to a substrate (usually cells), allowing autoantibodies to bind to their target antigens. A secondary fluorescent antibody is then added, which binds to the autoantibodies, enabling visualization under a fluorescence microscope. This method is highly sensitive and allows for the detection of a wide range of autoantibodies, including ANA, which is frequently elevated in patients with SLE.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. ELISA: While enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) can be used for specific autoantibody detection, such as anti-dsDNA or anti-Smith antibodies in SLE, it is not the most commonly used technique for initial ANA screening, which is typically done using indirect immunofluorescence.

 

Option B. FISH (Fluorescence in situ hybridization): Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a cytogenetic technique used to detect chromosomal abnormalities and is not typically used for autoantibody detection.

 

Option C. Direct immunofluorescence: Direct immunofluorescence is used to detect antibody or complement deposition directly in tissues, such as in skin biopsies, but it is not commonly used for detecting circulating autoantibodies in the blood, as in the case of ANA.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Indirect immunofluorescence is the preferred and most commonly used technique for detecting anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA), which are often present in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

questions.stem: Hepatitis B is associated with increased risk of liver cancer in patients because of:

options.label: A
options.text: Increased survival time in host cells

options.label: C
options.text: Enhanced release of tumor suppressor gene products

options.label: D
options.text: Intergration of viral RNA with host DNA

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) High rate of hepatocyte proliferation

 

Chronic Hepatitis B infection leads to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) primarily due to the continuous cycle of liver damage and regeneration. The virus induces chronic liver inflammation, which leads to repeated cycles of hepatocyte injury, death, and compensatory hepatocyte proliferation. This increased hepatocyte turnover creates a higher likelihood of accumulating genetic mutations, which can result in the development of liver cancer over time.

 

Furthermore, the Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a DNA virus (not RNA), and it integrates into the host genome, but this integration is not the main reason for the heightened cancer risk. The persistent hepatocyte proliferation and the accompanying inflammatory microenvironment are key factors leading to oncogenesis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Increased survival time in host cells: While HBV can persist in hepatocytes for a long time, this alone does not explain the higher risk of cancer. The repeated cycles of damage and repair, along with mutation accumulation during hepatocyte proliferation, are more critical in cancer development.

 

Option C. Enhanced release of tumor suppressor gene products: This statement is incorrect. Tumor suppressor genes normally work to prevent cancer, and a reduction, rather than enhancement, of these products would promote cancer development.

 

Option D. Integration of viral RNA with host DNA: HBV is a DNA virus, not an RNA virus. While HBV DNA can integrate into the host genome, the high rate of hepatocyte proliferation due to chronic liver injury is the main mechanism for the increased cancer risk.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Hepatitis B infection leads to liver cancer primarily due to the high rate of hepatocyte proliferation that occurs as part of the liver’s compensatory response to chronic injury and inflammation, increasing the risk of mutations and oncogenesis.

questions.stem: Due to which phenomenon do B cells express IgM and IgD antibodies at the same time?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Alternative RNA splicing

 

B cells express both IgM and IgD antibodies on their surface simultaneously during their development, and this co-expression occurs due to a process called alternative RNA splicing. Both IgM and IgD are encoded by the same primary RNA transcript, which is derived from the rearranged heavy chain locus. The choice between expressing IgM or IgD is not due to DNA rearrangement or somatic mutation, but rather the alternative splicing of the mRNA.

 

This allows the same B cell to produce both IgM and IgD antibodies that share the same antigen specificity, a phenomenon seen in mature, naïve B cells.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Somatic hypermutation: Somatic hypermutation is the process that introduces point mutations in the variable region of immunoglobulin genes to increase antibody affinity, but it does not explain the simultaneous expression of IgM and IgD.

 

Option C. Affinity maturation: Affinity maturation refers to the process by which B cells produce antibodies with increased affinity for their antigen through somatic hypermutation, but this process does not involve the co-expression of IgM and IgD.

 

Option D. Allelic exclusion: Allelic exclusion ensures that each B cell expresses immunoglobulin from only one allele (either maternal or paternal) for the heavy chain and light chain loci, ensuring antigen specificity. It does not account for the simultaneous expression of IgM and IgD.

 

Educational Objective:

 

B cells express both IgM and IgD antibodies on their surface simultaneously due to alternative RNA splicing, a mechanism that allows the same RNA transcript to be spliced in different ways, resulting in the production of both antibody types from the same gene.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old young female presents with a bleeding disorder. Upon taking a detailed history, she reveals that her father and sister also have the same bleeding disorder. Which is the most likely disorder in her?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Von Willebrand disease

 

Von Willebrand disease (vWD) is the most likely diagnosis in this case, given the autosomal inheritance pattern and the fact that both males and females in the family are affected. vWD is the most common inherited bleeding disorder and affects both genders equally. It is caused by a deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor (vWF), which plays a critical role in platelet adhesion and stabilization of factor VIII.

 

Key points:

 

  • Both males and females are affected (as seen in the patient’s father and sister).
  • It is the most common bleeding disorder.
  • vWD can present with mucocutaneous bleeding, easy bruising, and prolonged bleeding time.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hemophilia A: Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder, typically affecting males, with females being carriers. Since the patient is female and the disease is present in both her father and sister, Hemophilia A is less likely.

 

Option B. Christmas disease: Also known as Hemophilia B, this is another X-linked recessive disorder affecting mostly males. The inheritance pattern described (both a father and a sister being affected) is inconsistent with an X-linked condition.

 

Option D. Factor XI deficiency: Factor XI deficiency is inherited in either an autosomal dominant or recessive pattern and affects both genders. However, it is much rarer than von Willebrand disease, making it a less likely diagnosis in this scenario. 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Von Willebrand disease is the most likely diagnosis in a young female with a bleeding disorder affecting both males and females in the family, following an autosomal inheritance pattern.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old African American male presents to the emergency department with severe pain in his arms and legs. He reports a history of recurrent episodes of pain in various parts of his body, often triggered by dehydration. On examination, he has tenderness over his extremities, and his spleen is palpable 2 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies reveal a hemoglobin level of 7.5 g/dL, reticulocytosis, and abnormally shaped erythrocytes on a peripheral blood smear. Which of the following is true about such cells?

options.label: A
options.text: Low mechanical fragility, low osmotic fragility

options.label: B
options.text: High mechanical fragility, high osmotic fragility

options.label: C
options.text: Low mechanical fragility, high osmotic fragility

options.label: D
options.text: High mechanical fragility, low osmotic fragility

questions.answerText: High mechanical fragility, low osmotic fragility
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) High mechanical fragility, low osmotic fragility

 

The patient's clinical presentation, including recurrent pain episodes triggered by dehydration and abnormal shaped erythrocytes on blood smear, is consistent with sickle cell anemia. In sickle cell anemia, hemoglobin S (HbS) causes red blood cells (RBCs) to assume a sickled shape under conditions like dehydration or hypoxia, leading to vaso-occlusive crises and pain.

 

In sickle cell disease, these abnormally shaped RBCs are mechanically fragile, meaning they are prone to rupture when passing through narrow capillaries or splenic sinusoids. However, these cells are less susceptible to osmotic lysis than normal RBCs, meaning they exhibit low osmotic fragility. This is because the sickled cells are more rigid and less permeable to water.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Low mechanical fragility, low osmotic fragility: This is incorrect because sickled cells have high mechanical fragility due to their abnormal shape and rigidity, which makes them prone to destruction.

 

Option B. High mechanical fragility, high osmotic fragility: This is incorrect because, although sickled cells have high mechanical fragility, their osmotic fragility is low, not high.

 

Option C. Low mechanical fragility, high osmotic fragility: This is incorrect as sickle cells exhibit high mechanical fragility but low osmotic fragility.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In sickle cell anemia, the abnormal red blood cells exhibit high mechanical fragility but low osmotic fragility, which is characteristic of this disease and its complications, such as hemolytic anemia and vaso-occlusive crises.

 

What happens to red cells in SCD?

 

  • Due to a mutation in the β-globin gene (Glu→Val at position 6), hemoglobin S (HbS) forms.
  • Under low oxygen, dehydration, or acidosis, HbS polymerizes → RBCs become sickled.

 

Sickled RBCs:

 

  • Are less flexible
  • Prone to mechanical damage in microvasculature
  • Removed prematurely → hemolytic anemia

 

 

  • High mechanical fragility → RBCs easily damaged in circulation
  • Low osmotic fragility → Cells resist lysis in hypotonic solutions due to dehydration

 

Note:

 

This is opposite of hereditary spherocytosis, where osmotic fragility is increased.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old male recently diagnosed with membranous glomerulopathy experiences sudden onset flank pain and gross hematuria. On physical examination, there is a left-sided varicocele. Urinalysis reveals increased proteinuria. This patient’s condition is most likely related to urinary loss of which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Antithrombin III

 

The patient's presentation of membranous glomerulopathy, sudden onset flank pain, gross hematuria, and left-sided varicocele strongly suggests renal vein thrombosis (RVT), a known complication of nephrotic syndrome. Membranous glomerulopathy is one of the most common causes of nephrotic syndrome in adults, and nephrotic syndrome increases the risk of thromboembolism, particularly renal vein thrombosis.

 

The primary mechanism for this increased risk of thrombosis in nephrotic syndrome is the urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins, specifically Antithrombin III (ATIII). The loss of ATIII, which normally inhibits coagulation, leads to a hypercoagulable state, predisposing the patient to venous thrombosis, including renal vein thrombosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Albumin: While albumin loss is a hallmark of nephrotic syndrome, leading to hypoalbuminemia and edema, it is not directly responsible for the thrombotic events. The increased risk of thrombosis is primarily due to the loss of antithrombin III rather than albumin.

 

Option B. Immune globulins: Loss of immune globulins in nephrotic syndrome may predispose patients to infections, but it is not directly related to the development of thrombosis.

 

Option D. Lipoproteins: Elevated lipoproteins are seen in nephrotic syndrome, contributing to hyperlipidemia, but they do not directly cause thrombosis. The hypercoagulable state is primarily due to the loss of antithrombin III and other anticoagulants.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In patients with membranous glomerulopathy and nephrotic syndrome, the urinary loss of antithrombin III is a key factor in the development of renal vein thrombosis and other thromboembolic complications.

questions.stem: In a known case of breast cancer, Fluorescent In-Situ Hybridization (FISH) for gene amplification will be done based on which of the following immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining for HER2/Neu?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 2

 

In breast cancer, HER2/Neu status is often assessed using immunohistochemistry (IHC) to determine if the tumor overexpresses the HER2 receptor. IHC scores are used to guide further testing or treatment decisions:

 

  • Score 3+: Strong, complete membrane staining in >10% of tumor cells, indicating HER2 positivity. No further testing is required as this is considered HER2 positive.
  • Score 0 or 1+: Little to no membrane staining, indicating HER2 negativity. No further testing is required.
  • Score 2+: Equivocal staining. This result is uncertain, and further testing is required to clarify the HER2 status. This is where FISH (Fluorescent In-Situ Hybridization) is performed to check for gene amplification of HER2/Neu.

 

FISH testing is recommended for equivocal (2+) IHC results to definitively determine HER2 gene amplification.

 

Educational Objective:

 

FISH is recommended when an IHC score of 2+ is observed in breast cancer cases to confirm HER2 gene amplification.

 

What is HER2/Neu?

 

  • HER2 (Human Epidermal growth factor Receptor 2) is a proto-oncogene on chromosome 17.
  • It encodes a transmembrane tyrosine kinase receptor.

 

Amplification or overexpression of HER2 occurs in about 15–20% of breast cancers and is associated with:

 

  • More aggressive disease
  • Poorer prognosis
  • But importantly — better response to targeted therapy (e.g., trastuzumab, pertuzumab)
  • HER2 Testing: IHC and FISH
  • First step: Immunohistochemistry (IHC)

 

HER2 protein overexpression is assessed on tumor tissue using IHC. Results are scored as:

 

 

  • Second step: FISH (Fluorescent In Situ Hybridization)
  • FISH directly tests for HER2 gene amplification in the DNA.
  • Used when IHC is 2+ (equivocal), because IHC can't clearly determine overexpression.
  • FISH provides definitive yes/no on gene amplification.

questions.stem: Which of the following is incorrect about invasive lobular carcinoma of the breast?

options.label: A
options.text: It is presenting as an occult primary

options.label: B
options.text: It is associated with familial gastric cancer

options.label: C
options.text: There is over-activity of CDH1 gene

options.label: D
options.text: It tends to be multifocal and bilateral.

questions.answerText: There is over-activity of CDH1 gene
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) There is over-activity of CDH1 gene

 

This statement is incorrect. In invasive lobular carcinoma, the CDH1 gene, which encodes the protein E-cadherin, is typically underactive or inactivated, not overactive. E-cadherin is responsible for cell adhesion, and its loss leads to the characteristic discohesive pattern of invasive lobular carcinoma cells.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It is presenting as an occult primary: This is correct. Invasive lobular carcinoma can present as an occult primary due to its tendency to grow in a diffuse pattern, which makes it difficult to detect on imaging, and it can be subtle on physical examination.

 

Option B. It is associated with familial gastric cancer: This is correct. Mutations in the CDH1 gene are associated with both invasive lobular carcinoma of the breast and familial diffuse gastric cancer.

 

Option D. It tends to be multifocal and bilateral: This is correct. Invasive lobular carcinoma has a higher tendency to be multifocal (occurring in more than one location within the same breast) and bilateral (affecting both breasts) compared to other types of breast cancer.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In invasive lobular carcinoma, the CDH1 gene is typically underactive, leading to a loss of E-cadherin function. This loss is associated with both lobular carcinoma of the breast and familial diffuse gastric cancer, and the tumor often presents as multifocal and bilateral.

questions.stem: Pick the correct statements about hemolytic anemia: Sickle cell anemia has high osmotic fragility and high mechanical fragilityIncreased HbA2 is seen with iron deficiency anemiaMentzer index helps in the differentiation of thalassemia trait from iron deficiency anemiaDonath Landsteiner antibody is seen in cold hemolysin disease
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 3 and 4

 

3. Mentzer index helps in the differentiation of thalassemia trait from iron deficiency anemia:
This is correct. The Mentzer index is calculated as the MCV (mean corpuscular volume) divided by the RBC count. A Mentzer index of <13 suggests thalassemia, while an index of >13 suggests iron deficiency anemia.

 

4. Donath Landsteiner antibody is seen in cold hemolysin disease:
This is correct. The Donath-Landsteiner antibody is a characteristic finding in paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH), which is also known as cold hemolysin disease. It is an autoantibody that binds to RBCs in cold temperatures and causes hemolysis upon rewarming.

 

Other Options:

 

1. Sickle cell anemia has high osmotic fragility and high mechanical fragility: This is incorrect. Sickle cells have high mechanical fragility but low osmotic fragility. They are more prone to mechanical damage as they pass through narrow capillaries, but they are less susceptible to osmotic lysis.

 

2. Increased HbA2 is seen with iron deficiency anemia: This is incorrect. Increased HbA2 is a characteristic of beta-thalassemia trait, not iron deficiency anemia. In iron deficiency anemia, HbA2 levels are usually normal or even decreased.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The Mentzer index helps differentiate thalassemia trait from iron deficiency anemia.
  • Donath-Landsteiner antibody is a marker for cold hemolysin disease (paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria).

questions.stem: A 32-year-old female presents with lymphadenopathy and night sweats. A lymph node biopsy shows Reed-Sternberg cells with inflammatory cells in the background. Flow cytometry of the lymph node specimen is most likely to reveal which of the following findings?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Clonal expansion of B lymphocytes

 

The presence of Reed-Sternberg cells in the lymph node biopsy is a classic feature of Hodgkin's lymphoma. Reed-Sternberg cells are derived from B cells, specifically post-germinal center B cells. These cells are abnormal and proliferate, leading to the development of Hodgkin's lymphoma.

 

Hodgkin's lymphoma is a B-cell malignancy, and thus, clonal expansion of B lymphocytes is the most likely finding on flow cytometry.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Clonal expansion of T lymphocytes: Hodgkin's lymphoma is a B-cell malignancy, not a T-cell disorder. Therefore, clonal expansion of T lymphocytes is not expected.

 

Option C. Increased CD4 ratio: An increased CD4 ratio may be seen in certain immune conditions, but it is not a hallmark of Hodgkin's lymphoma.

 

Option D. Loss of CD19 expression: CD19 is a B-cell marker, and while Reed-Sternberg cells are derived from B cells, they often lose some of their typical B-cell markers, but the diagnosis of Hodgkin's lymphoma is based on Reed-Sternberg cells and clonal B-cell expansion rather than complete loss of B-cell markers like CD19.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Hodgkin's lymphoma is characterized by the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells, which are derived from B cells, making the clonal expansion of B lymphocytes the most likely finding on flow cytometry.

questions.stem: A research study investigates metabolic changes in cancer cells. Which of the following cellular components is most likely to be upregulated in cancer cells exhibiting the Warburg effect?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Cytoplasmic ribosomes

 

The Warburg effect describes how cancer cells preferentially use aerobic glycolysis for energy production, even in the presence of sufficient oxygen. This metabolic shift favors the production of ATP and building blocks for cell growth and division from glycolysis, rather than the more efficient oxidative phosphorylation that occurs in mitochondria.

 

Increased glycolysis in cancer cells leads to an enhanced demand for protein synthesis machinery to support rapid cell growth and division. Cytoplasmic ribosomes, which are responsible for protein synthesis, are upregulated in cancer cells to meet this increased demand. The higher ribosomal activity supports the production of enzymes involved in glycolysis, as well as other proteins necessary for cell proliferation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Mitochondria: While mitochondria are important for energy production through oxidative phosphorylation, cancer cells downregulate this pathway in favor of glycolysis (Warburg effect), so there is no significant upregulation of mitochondrial activity in these cells.

 

Option C. Peroxisomes: Peroxisomes are involved in lipid metabolism and detoxification, but they are not directly involved in the metabolic changes driven by the Warburg effect.

 

Option D. Lysosomes: Lysosomes are involved in waste processing and recycling cellular components but are not directly associated with the increased metabolic demands and glycolytic pathway seen in cancer cells exhibiting the Warburg effect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Warburg effect leads to increased cytoplasmic ribosomal activity to support the elevated protein synthesis needed for rapid cell proliferation and metabolic shifts in cancer cells.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old female with a history of von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease presents with abdominal discomfort and elevated blood pressure. Imaging reveals multiple clear cell renal cell carcinomas in both kidneys. Genetic testing confirms a mutation in the short arm of chromosome 3. What is the most important factor contributing to the development of renal cell carcinoma in this patient?

options.label: C
options.text: Long-term use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)

options.label: D
options.text: Inactivation of the VHL tumor suppressor gene

questions.answerText: Inactivation of the VHL tumor suppressor gene
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Inactivation of the VHL tumor suppressor gene

 

This patient has von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease, which is caused by mutations in the VHL tumor suppressor gene located on the short arm of chromosome 3 (3p). VHL disease predisposes patients to multiple tumors, including clear cell renal cell carcinoma (RCC), which is the most common subtype of RCC. The VHL gene plays a critical role in regulating cell growth and angiogenesis by targeting hypoxia-inducible factors (HIF) for degradation. When the VHL gene is inactivated, these factors accumulate, leading to uncontrolled cell growth and tumor formation.

 

Although cigarette smoking and other environmental factors can contribute to the risk of developing RCC, the most important factor in this patient's case is the inactivation of the VHL tumor suppressor gene.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cigarette smoking: While smoking is a well-known risk factor for RCC, the primary cause in this patient is the VHL mutation, not smoking.

 

Option B. Occupational exposure to asbestos: Asbestos is more commonly associated with lung diseases like mesothelioma, not RCC. It is not relevant to this patient’s case.

 

Option C. Long-term use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs): Long-term NSAID use can increase the risk of chronic kidney disease, but it is not a primary factor in the development of RCC in this patient.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease, the development of renal cell carcinoma is primarily due to the inactivation of the VHL tumor suppressor gene, leading to uncontrolled cell growth, particularly in clear cell RCC.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of liver cirrhosis presents to the emergency department with gastrointestinal bleeding. Laboratory tests reveal prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT). Thromboelastography (TEG) is performed and shows a prolonged reaction time (R-time), decreased angle (α-angle), and reduced maximum amplitude (MA). Which of the following best explains these TEG findings?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Hypocoagulability

 

The patient’s history of liver cirrhosis, prolonged PT and aPTT, and the TEG findings all point towards a state of hypocoagulability.

 

  • Prolonged R-time indicates a delay in clot formation, which suggests a deficiency in clotting factors.
  • A decreased α-angle suggests reduced fibrinogen activity or fibrin formation, further indicating a deficiency in clotting.
  • A reduced maximum amplitude (MA) indicates platelet dysfunction or reduced clot strength, showing that the platelets are not functioning optimally.

 

These findings are consistent with hypocoagulability, a condition where the blood has a reduced ability to clot, which is common in patients with liver cirrhosis due to decreased production of clotting factors and fibrinogen, as well as platelet dysfunction.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hypercoagulability: This would be seen with shortened R-time and increased MA on TEG, reflecting increased clotting potential, which is not supported by the patient's findings.

 

Option C. Platelet dysfunction: While platelet dysfunction could explain the reduced MA, it would not explain the prolonged R-time and decreased α-angle, which indicate problems with clotting factors and fibrinogen, not just platelets.

 

Option D. Fibrinolysis: Fibrinolysis would typically present with a normal R-time and α-angle but a decreased MA and lysis at the end of the TEG tracing. This is not the case here, as the findings suggest issues with the clotting cascade and platelet function.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The prolonged R-time, decreased α-angle, and reduced MA seen on TEG, combined with a history of liver cirrhosis and prolonged PT/aPTT, indicate a state of hypocoagulability. Liver cirrhosis impairs the production of clotting factors, fibrinogen, and platelet function, leading to a bleeding tendency.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old patient with metastatic lung cancer is treated with a targeted therapy directed against an oncogenic mutation specific to their tumor. Despite a poor overall prognosis, the patient experiences a remarkable response to the treatment, with a significant reduction in tumor size. Which of the following concepts best explains this phenomenon?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Oncogene addiction

 

The concept of oncogene addiction refers to the phenomenon where a tumor becomes highly dependent on a single oncogenic pathway or mutation for its survival and proliferation, even though multiple genetic alterations may be present. In this case, the patient's tumor likely harbors a specific oncogenic mutation that the targeted therapy is designed to inhibit. By blocking this critical mutation, the therapy effectively suppresses the growth and survival of the cancer cells, leading to a significant reduction in tumor size.

 

Despite the complexity of cancer, many tumors become reliant on a single oncogenic driver, and targeted therapies can lead to dramatic responses, even in cases of metastatic cancer, by disrupting this crucial pathway.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Metastatic suppression: This refers to the ability to control or suppress metastasis but does not directly explain the patient’s remarkable response to the targeted therapy. The response in this case is due to inhibition of the specific oncogenic mutation rather than suppression of metastasis.

 

Option B. Tumor heterogeneity: Tumor heterogeneity refers to the presence of diverse cancer cell populations with different genetic mutations within the same tumor. While heterogeneity can explain differences in response to treatment, it does not explain the remarkable response seen in this patient, which is better attributed to oncogene addiction.

 

Option D. Tumor microenvironment modulation: Modulation of the tumor microenvironment involves altering the surrounding non-cancerous cells, immune cells, and extracellular matrix that support tumor growth. While important in cancer biology, this concept is not the main reason for the dramatic tumor shrinkage in response to a targeted therapy.

 

Educational Objective:

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with redness, swelling, and pain in his left ankle. He reports a recent history of trauma to the ankle. Physical examination reveals erythema, warmth, and swelling localized to the left ankle joint. Laboratory tests show an elevated white blood cell count with a predominance of neutrophils. Which of the following cellular events is the primary characteristic of the acute inflammatory response in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Neutrophil recruitment

 

The patient's presentation of redness, swelling, and pain in the ankle, along with neutrophil predominance, is indicative of acute inflammation, which is the body's initial response to injury or infection. The primary cellular event during the acute inflammatory response is the recruitment of neutrophils to the site of injury or infection. Neutrophils are the first responders, arriving within hours to engulf pathogens, debris, or damaged tissue.

 

  • Neutrophil recruitment is the hallmark of acute inflammation, where they help combat infection or clean up damaged tissue.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Macrophage infiltration: Macrophages are involved later in the inflammatory process and are more prominent in chronic inflammation. They help in tissue repair and the resolution of inflammation.

 

Option B. Lymphocyte activation: Lymphocytes, primarily T and B cells, play a major role in chronic inflammation and the adaptive immune response, not in the early stages of acute inflammation.

 

Option D. Fibroblast proliferation: Fibroblasts are involved in tissue repair and scarring, and their proliferation is more characteristic of the healing phase rather than the acute inflammatory response.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In acute inflammation, the primary cellular response is neutrophil recruitment, which is the body's first line of defense to address the injury or infection. Other immune cells, such as macrophages and lymphocytes, are more involved in chronic or later stages of inflammation.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with a painless neck mass. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mass reveals papillary structures with ground-glass nuclei and nuclear grooves. Immunohistochemical staining shows positive staining for thyroglobulin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC)

 

The clinical presentation and pathological findings are characteristic of Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC). Key features include:

 

  • Painless neck mass: A common presentation of PTC.
  • Papillary structures, ground-glass ("Orphan Annie eye") nuclei, and nuclear grooves are classic cytological features seen in PTC.
  • Positive staining for thyroglobulin: This is typical in well-differentiated thyroid cancers, including PTC, since thyroglobulin is a marker of thyroid origin.

 

Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common type of thyroid cancer, and it is often associated with a favorable prognosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Medullary thyroid carcinoma: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular (C-cells) and is associated with calcitonin production, not thyroglobulin. It does not present with the papillary structures or nuclear features described here.

 

Option B. Follicular adenoma: Follicular adenomas are benign thyroid tumors that do not typically show the papillary structures or nuclear features such as grooves and ground-glass appearance seen in PTC.

 

Option D. Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is a highly aggressive and undifferentiated form of thyroid cancer. It presents as a rapidly enlarging, often painful neck mass, and it lacks the characteristic nuclear features of PTC.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is identified by its characteristic papillary structures, ground-glass ("Orphan Annie eye") nuclei, and nuclear grooves, along with positive immunohistochemical staining for thyroglobulin.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old alcoholic is admitted to the hospital with congestive heart failure. Physical examination shows bilateral basal crackles, increased jugular venous pressure, ascites, and peripheral edema. Chest x-ray demonstrates cardiomegaly. Laboratory testing shows mild thrombocytopenia and prolonged prothrombin time (PT). The patient is given intramuscular vitamin K, but his prothrombin time is still prolonged. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s prolonged prothrombin time?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Coagulation factor VII deficiency

 

The patient presents with congestive heart failure (CHF), which can lead to congestive hepatomegaly (liver congestion). This congestion impairs liver function, reducing its ability to produce clotting factors. The liver is the primary site of synthesis for vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (factors II, VII, IX, and X), as well as other coagulation factors.

 

  • Prolonged PT indicates a defect in the extrinsic coagulation pathway, which involves factor VII. Factor VII has the shortest half-life among clotting factors, so a deficiency in this factor often leads to an early prolongation of PT.
  • Vitamin K administration did not correct the prolonged PT, suggesting that the problem is not due to vitamin K deficiency but rather due to hepatic dysfunction.
  • CHF and liver congestion impair the liver's ability to synthesize clotting factors, including factor VII, leading to the observed prolonged PT.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Dietary vitamin K deficiency: If this were the cause, administration of vitamin K should have corrected the prolonged PT. Since it did not, dietary deficiency is not the issue.

 

Option B. Defective platelets: Defective platelets would result in bleeding abnormalities but would not cause prolonged PT. PT measures clotting factor function, not platelet function.

 

Option D. Coagulation factor VIII deficiency: Factor VIII is part of the intrinsic pathway, which is assessed by aPTT, not PT. Factor VIII deficiency is associated with hemophilia A, which would not explain this patient's prolonged PT.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The patient's prolonged PT is most likely due to coagulation factor VII deficiency caused by hepatic dysfunction secondary to congestive heart failure. Factor VII is the first factor to become deficient due to its short half-life, leading to the observed coagulation abnormalities.

questions.stem: Animals, especially rodents, subjected to chronic inhalation exposure to formaldehyde develop nasal squamous cell carcinomas. Decreased activity of which of the following genes is likely to be found on cytogenetic studies of the tumor cells?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) p53

 

The p53 gene is a well-known tumor suppressor gene that plays a critical role in regulating the cell cycle, DNA repair, and apoptosis. When the activity of p53 is decreased or lost, cells with damaged DNA can continue to proliferate, leading to the development of cancer. In the context of nasal squamous cell carcinomas caused by chronic exposure to carcinogens like formaldehyde, a decrease in p53 activity allows cells to evade normal regulatory mechanisms, contributing to tumor formation.

 

  • p53 mutations or decreased activity are commonly associated with various cancers, including those induced by environmental carcinogens.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. BCR-ABL: The BCR-ABL fusion gene is associated with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) and is not typically involved in squamous cell carcinomas.

 

Option B. Ras: Ras is a proto-oncogene that, when overactive, can lead to uncontrolled cell growth. However, the question specifically asks about decreased activity, making Ras less likely to be the answer.

 

Option C. Erb-B2 (HER2): Erb-B2 (HER2) is another proto-oncogene associated with breast and other cancers, where its overexpression leads to tumorigenesis. It is not related to decreased activity in the context of squamous cell carcinoma.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The development of nasal squamous cell carcinoma following chronic exposure to formaldehyde is most likely associated with decreased activity of the p53 tumor suppressor gene, which plays a key role in preventing the proliferation of damaged cells.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old college student is brought to the emergency department by her friends after they found her drowsy and confused. She admits to taking an overdose of acetaminophen about 18 hours ago following a breakup. She is experiencing nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Her liver function tests are markedly elevated, and she is jaundiced. There is no history of liver disease or alcohol abuse. Which of the following best describes the pathophysiological mechanism of her hepatic injury?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Direct hepatotoxicity from free radicals

 

The patient presents with classic symptoms of acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose, including nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes. Acetaminophen overdose leads to hepatic injury through direct hepatotoxicity caused by the accumulation of a toxic metabolite, N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI).

 

Normally, NAPQI is detoxified by glutathione in the liver. However, in an overdose, glutathione stores become depleted, and the excess NAPQI binds to liver proteins, generating free radicals and causing direct hepatocyte damage, leading to acute liver injury.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ischemic hepatocyte damage: Ischemic damage occurs in conditions of reduced blood flow to the liver, such as shock or severe hypotension. This mechanism is not relevant in acetaminophen overdose.

 

Option C. Autoimmune-mediated liver injury: Autoimmune liver injury is caused by the immune system attacking liver cells, often involving autoantibodies. This mechanism is unrelated to acetaminophen toxicity, which is caused by direct hepatotoxicity.

 

Option D. Cholestatic liver injury: Cholestatic injury refers to impaired bile flow, which is not a primary mechanism in acetaminophen toxicity. The injury in this case is due to toxic metabolite buildup rather than bile obstruction.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Acetaminophen overdose leads to direct hepatotoxicity through the accumulation of toxic metabolites (NAPQI), which causes free radical formation and subsequent liver cell damage. This is the primary mechanism of liver injury in this case.

questions.stem: What can be the mechanism by which the phagolysosome causes cell death in autophagy?

options.label: A
options.text: Is both intra and extra cellular

options.label: B
options.text: Can fuse with other organelles directly

options.label: C
options.text: Fuses with lysosome to form autophagolysosome

options.label: D
options.text: It is a single membrane structure

questions.answerText: Fuses with lysosome to form autophagolysosome
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Fuses with lysosome to form autophagolysosome

 

In the process of autophagy, a phagosome (or autophagosome) forms and engulfs damaged organelles or cellular components. This autophagosome then fuses with a lysosome to form an autophagolysosome, where the contents are degraded by lysosomal enzymes. This is a critical step in the degradation and recycling of cellular materials, and in cases of excessive autophagy, it can lead to cell death by overwhelming the cell’s ability to maintain homeostasis.

 

  • Phagolysosome formation involves the fusion of the autophagosome with the lysosome, which is key to the degradation process.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Is both intra and extracellular: Autophagy is an intracellular process that occurs within the cell. It does not involve extracellular mechanisms.

 

Option B. Can fuse with other organelles directly: While autophagosomes may engulf damaged organelles, they do not fuse with organelles directly. Instead, they fuse with lysosomes to form autophagolysosomes for degradation.

 

Option D. It is a single membrane structure: The autophagosome is a double-membrane structure, not single membrane. The double membrane is one of the distinguishing features of autophagosomes in the autophagic process.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In autophagy, the autophagosome fuses with a lysosome to form an autophagolysosome, where cellular materials are degraded. This process is essential for the breakdown and recycling of damaged organelles and can lead to cell death if autophagy is excessive.

questions.stem: All of the following features are observed in pleomorphic adenoma except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Perineural invasion

 

Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common benign tumor of the salivary glands, particularly the parotid gland. It is a mixed tumor, meaning it contains multiple cell types, including myoepithelial cells and epithelial cells, as well as mesenchymal elements that can show chondroid (cartilage-like) differentiation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Myoepithelial cells: Myoepithelial cells are a hallmark of pleomorphic adenoma and contribute to its mixed cellular composition.

 

Option B. Keratin pearls: Keratin production can be observed due to the presence of epithelial cells in pleomorphic adenomas.

 

Option C. Chondroid differentiation: The tumor often has areas of cartilaginous differentiation, which is one of its defining features.

 

However, perineural invasion is not characteristic of pleomorphic adenoma. This feature is more commonly associated with malignant tumors, such as adenoid cystic carcinoma, which is known for its tendency to invade nerves.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Perineural invasion is not a feature of pleomorphic adenoma, which is a benign tumor. It is commonly seen in malignant tumors, such as adenoid cystic carcinoma.

questions.stem: An intracranial mass is removed from a 33-year-old male. The mass is composed of elongated cells that have regular, oval nuclei and demonstrate areas of dense and loose growth patterns. The cells show S-100 immunoreactivity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Schwannoma

 

The description of the tumor with elongated cells, regular oval nuclei, and alternating areas of dense (Antoni A) and loose (Antoni B) growth patterns, along with S-100 immunoreactivity, is characteristic of a schwannoma. Schwannomas are benign nerve sheath tumors that arise from Schwann cells, which express S-100 protein.

 

  • Antoni A and Antoni B areas: Schwannomas are known for their biphasic pattern, consisting of dense cellular areas (Antoni A) and loose myxoid areas (Antoni B).
  • S-100 immunoreactivity: S-100 is a marker for neural crest-derived cells, including Schwann cells, and is positive in schwannomas.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Meningioma: Meningiomas are characterized by whorled cell patterns and psammoma bodies. They typically do not show S-100 positivity, which is a marker for Schwann cells.

 

Option C. Metastatic lung cancer: Metastatic lung cancer can present as an intracranial mass, but it would not have the histologic features or S-100 positivity seen in schwannomas.

 

Option D. Optic glioma: Optic gliomas are associated with astrocytes and do not display the biphasic Antoni A and B patterns or S-100 positivity that are characteristic of schwannomas.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A schwannoma is characterized by Antoni A and B areas and S-100 immunoreactivity, which distinguish it from other intracranial masses.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old female presents in the outpatient department reporting that she passes blood instead of urine during the night. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the PIGA gene. She undergoes a series of laboratory tests including the Ham test. What is the primary abnormality detected by the Ham test?

options.label: D
options.text: Lysis of RBCs in a mildly acidic pH

questions.answerText: Lysis of RBCs in a mildly acidic pH
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Lysis of RBCs in a mildly acidic pH

 

The Ham test is used to diagnose paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), a condition caused by a mutation in the PIGA gene, which leads to a deficiency in proteins like CD55 and CD59 that protect red blood cells (RBCs) from complement-mediated lysis.

 

In the Ham test, the patient's RBCs are exposed to an acidic environment, which activates the complement system. In PNH, the deficiency of protective proteins results in increased lysis of RBCs in a mildly acidic pH. The Ham test demonstrates the vulnerability of PNH RBCs to complement-mediated destruction under these conditions.

 

  • Lysis of RBCs in a mildly acidic pH is the primary abnormality detected by the Ham test.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Elevated LDH: While elevated LDH is a marker of hemolysis seen in PNH, the Ham test does not measure LDH levels directly.

 

Option B. Venous thrombosis: PNH is associated with an increased risk of venous thrombosis, but the Ham test specifically detects complement-mediated hemolysis, not thrombosis.

 

Option C. Deficiency of CD59 and CD55: The deficiency of CD59 and CD55 proteins is the underlying abnormality in PNH, but this is confirmed using flow cytometry, not the Ham test. The Ham test specifically measures RBC lysis in an acidic environment.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Ham test detects lysis of red blood cells in a mildly acidic pH, a hallmark of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), due to the deficiency of protective proteins like CD55 and CD59 on the RBC surface.

questions.stem: A patient has been diagnosed with a condition due to a DNA repair gene defect. He has hyperpigmentation on the skin and a higher risk of developing skin cancer, as indicated by his physician. Which of the following is a likely enzyme defect in the patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Nucleotide excision repair gene defect

 

The patient’s symptoms of hyperpigmentation, high sensitivity to UV light, and increased risk of skin cancer are indicative of Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP), a disorder caused by a defect in the nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway. This pathway is responsible for repairing DNA damage caused by UV radiation, specifically thymine dimers and other lesions formed on exposure to sunlight.

 

In XP, defects in genes responsible for nucleotide excision repair lead to the inability to repair UV-induced DNA damage, resulting in the symptoms described and a predisposition to skin cancer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Helicase: A defect in helicase is associated with Werner syndrome, which leads to premature aging but is not specifically linked to skin cancer or UV-induced DNA damage.

 

Option B. ATM gene: ATM gene defects are seen in Ataxia-Telangiectasia, which involves neurodegeneration, immunodeficiency, and an increased risk of leukemia and lymphoma, but not primarily skin cancer due to UV exposure.

 

Option C. MSH gene: MSH gene mutations are linked to Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer), involving mismatch repair deficiencies, and are more associated with colorectal and endometrial cancers, not skin cancer.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The nucleotide excision repair gene defect is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms in Xeroderma Pigmentosum, characterized by DNA repair failure after UV exposure, leading to hyperpigmentation and an increased risk of skin cancer.

 

What is Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP)?

 

XP is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by defects in DNA repair mechanisms, specifically:

 

  • Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) Pathway
  • This pathway is responsible for repairing UV-induced DNA damage — especially thymine dimers.
  • UV light causes pyrimidine dimers (typically thymine-thymine dimers), which distort the DNA helix.
  • Normally, these are removed by NER enzymes:
    • Damage is recognized
    • DNA is cut out (excised) around the lesion
    • DNA is resynthesized and ligated

 

In XP, NER genes (like XPA through XPG) are mutated → repair fails → mutations accumulate → early onset skin cancers.

 

  • NER defects also underlie Cockayne syndrome (but this causes growth failure, cachexia, and neurologic issues rather than cancer).
  • XP is unique in its strong cancer predisposition due to unrepaired UV damage.

questions.stemHtml: A 43-year-old man has complained of heartburn for the past 5 months. On physical examination, there are no abnormal findings. Upper GI endoscopy is performed. Biopsies are taken from an erythematous area of the lower esophageal mucosa. There is no mass lesion and no hemorrhage. The biopsies have the microscopic appearance shown here. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Epithelial metaplasia

 

The biopsy reveals intestinal metaplasia with glandular structures showing goblet cells in the lower esophagus, which is consistent with Barrett's esophagus. In this condition, squamous epithelium of the esophagus is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells, a process referred to as epithelial metaplasia. Barrett's esophagus is associated with chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and it increases the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

 

  • Heartburn and chronic reflux symptoms are common features of patients with Barrett’s esophagus.
  • Erythematous mucosa seen on endoscopy suggests inflammation and metaplasia in the esophagus, but not acute inflammation (A) or carcinoma (B).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Acute inflammation: Acute inflammation would show neutrophil infiltration and does not explain the presence of intestinal metaplasia observed in Barrett's esophagus.

 

Option B. Metastatic carcinoma: There is no evidence of malignancy in the biopsy. The histological findings are consistent with metaplasia, not carcinoma.

 

Option C. Glandular hyperplasia: Glandular hyperplasia refers to an increase in the number of glandular cells but does not explain the change from squamous to columnar epithelium seen in Barrett's esophagus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The histological findings of intestinal metaplasia (columnar epithelium with goblet cells) in the lower esophagus are consistent with Barrett's esophagus, which is caused by chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and is an example of epithelial metaplasia.
